chapters.title: Chapter 6: Liquidity Risk and Liquidity-Adjusted VaR

lessons.title: The Bid-Ask Spread and Market Impact Cost

children.text: The last lesson established that exiting a position rarely happens at exactly the marked price. This lesson quantifies exactly why, with two distinct costs: the bid-ask spread, a fixed cost every trade pays, and market impact, a cost that grows specifically with how large your order is relative to how much the market can actually absorb.
The Bid-Ask Spread: The Baseline Cost of Trading

body.label: Bid-Ask Spread
body.value: The gap between the highest price a buyer will pay (bid) and the lowest price a seller will accept (ask)
body.context: A one-way trade typically costs roughly half this spread, relative to the mid-price.

children.text: A liquid mid-cap NSE stock shows a bid of Rs 499.50 and an ask of Rs 500.50, a mid-price of Rs 500 and a spread of Rs 1.00, or 0.2% of the mid-price. Buying at the ask and immediately selling at the bid costs the full 0.2%, so a single one-way trade costs roughly half that, 0.1%, relative to the mid-price you were marking the position at.
Market Impact: The Cost of Being a Large Trader in a Small Pool

The bid-ask spread is a fixed cost, it applies whether you trade Rs 10,000 or Rs 1 crore. Market impact is different, it grows specifically as your order size approaches or exceeds what the market can normally absorb in a day. A widely used practitioner heuristic for this is the square-root impact model, which says price impact scales with the square root of your order's participation rate, not linearly with it.

body.caption: The square-root impact model. Sigma is the stock's daily volatility, Q is your order size, ADV is average daily traded value, k is an empirical constant, taken as 1 here for illustration. This is a simplified, widely cited heuristic, not a universal law, real execution desks calibrate k from their own trading data.

children.text: Worked Example: Two Order Sizes, Nonlinear Cost

body.caption: Setup: a mid-cap NSE stock, daily volatility 2%, average daily traded value Rs 5,00,00,000
Total one-way exit cost at two different order sizes

body.text: Doubling the order size from Rs 50,00,000 to Rs 1,00,00,000 does not double the market impact, it rises from 0.632% to 0.894%, a factor of exactly the square root of 2, about 1.41x, not 2x. This nonlinearity is precisely why execution desks split large orders into smaller pieces over time, VWAP or TWAP-style algorithms, rather than dumping the full size into the market at once, spreading a large order reduces average impact per rupee traded, even though it takes longer and carries its own timing risk.

children.text: A VaR figure for this Rs 1,00,00,000 position, computed the way Chapter 2 taught, marks the position at the current price and stops there. But actually exiting that position costs an additional 0.994% of its value, Rs 99,443, on top of whatever market move VaR was measuring. That gap is not a market risk, it is a liquidity cost, and it is exactly what the next lesson, Liquidity-Adjusted VaR, builds directly into the risk number instead of ignoring.

body.title: Compute Total Exit Cost
body.prompt: Using the same stock, sigma 2%, ADV Rs 5,00,00,000, and half-spread cost 0.1%, what is the total one-way exit cost, in rupees, for an order of Rs 2,00,00,000?
body.explanation: Participation rate = Rs 2,00,00,000 / Rs 5,00,00,000 = 40%. Market impact = 2% x sqrt(0.40) = 1.265%. Total cost = 0.1% + 1.265% = 1.365%, applied to Rs 2,00,00,000 gives approximately Rs 2,72,982. Notice this order, at 40% of ADV, is carrying a total cost rate nearly double the Rs 1 crore order's 0.994%, even though it is only twice the size, a direct consequence of the square-root scaling.

body.title: Deciding How to Execute a Large Order
body.scenario: A fund needs to exit a Rs 1,00,00,000 position in the mid-cap stock from this lesson's worked example today, and is deciding between selling the entire position in one large order immediately, or splitting it into five smaller orders spread across the trading day.
body.prompt: Based on the square-root impact model, why would splitting the order likely reduce total execution cost, and what risk does splitting introduce instead?
body.modelAnswer: Splitting the order into five smaller pieces, each roughly Rs 20,00,000, reduces the participation rate of each individual trade, and because impact scales with the square root of participation rather than linearly, five smaller trades executed separately typically produce a lower combined impact cost than one large trade of the same total size. The trade-off is timing risk, called execution risk, spreading the sale across the day means the stock's price could move adversely for unrelated reasons before all five pieces are filled, so the fund is trading a known, calculable impact cost against an uncertain, but potentially smaller or larger, price move over the execution window.

body.text: The bid-ask spread is the toll everyone pays. Market impact is the toll only large orders pay, and it grows with the square root of size, not the size itself, which is exactly why how you trade a position can matter almost as much as what you trade.

points: The bid-ask spread is a fixed, size-independent cost, roughly half the spread for a one-way trade, relative to the mid-price.
Market impact grows with the square root of an order's participation rate relative to average daily traded value, not linearly, so doubling order size raises impact by only about 1.41x, not 2x.
A Rs 1 crore order at 20% of ADV in the worked example carried a total one-way exit cost of Rs 99,443, purely from spread and impact, a cost a standard mark-to-market VaR figure never accounts for.
Because impact is nonlinear in size, splitting a large order into smaller pieces over time typically reduces total execution cost, at the price of taking on execution timing risk instead.

The next lesson builds this exit cost directly into the VaR calculation itself, producing a Liquidity-Adjusted VaR figure that reflects what a position would actually cost to unwind, not just what it is currently marked at.
